_: advice — what `bash-advise.py` tells the AGENT when the gate returns ASK.
This file changes no verdict. It cannot allow, deny or rewrite a call; it only
produces a sentence. That is why it is NOT on the Edit/Write deny list that
the hooks, the profiles and rules.json are on — an agent that edits its own
advice has misled itself and nothing else.
One entry: {id, match, instead, why}. `match` is searched (not fullmatched)
against each segment the ALLOW rules rejected; the first hit wins, so put the
specific shapes above the general ones. `instead` must name a form that is
genuinely on this project's whitelist, or say plainly that none exists — an
entry that invents a spelling sends the agent hunting, which is the failure
this hook was written to stop.
Two entry kinds, and keep them distinguishable:
a rewrite  — an allowed form does the same work. Name it.
a real ask — the prompt IS the design (it discards work, deletes, pushes,
installs). Then `instead` says what the human needs to hear
before approving, not how to get around the prompt.
This file is a starting point. Curate it from
`permission-audit.py --report`: every shape on that list either earns a rule

advice.instead: nothing — this prompt is the design. Before it, say which files will be overwritten and whether any of them has uncommitted edits (`git status --short PATH`, which is allowed).
advice.why: checking a path out of a ref discards that file's working-tree changes and git keeps no copy, so the human is the only undo

advice.instead: git switch BRANCH, or git switch -c BRANCH to create one
advice.why: plain `git checkout X` is off the list because `git checkout src/File.ts` has the same spelling and throws that file's edits away; `switch` cannot be handed a path

advice.instead: drop the -C and run the bare `git VERB` if the target is this checkout. For another repository there is no allowed form unless this project added one.
advice.why: every git allow rule is anchored on `git VERB`, with no tolerance for the -C prefix

advice.instead: nothing — pushing is the human's call. Name the branch and the remote in one line so the approval is informed.
advice.why: a push is the first irreversible step outside this machine

advice.instead: nothing — deletion always prompts. Say what the file is and what still references it (an allowed `git grep` will tell you) before asking.
advice.why: an equivalent turns a stop into a detour, and there is no equivalent for removing a file

advice.instead: for a command you started in the background, read its output with the Monitor tool instead of inspecting the process table.
advice.why: the read-only allow set covers the filesystem but was never extended to the process table

advice.instead: drop the variable: put the literal value in the command, or make the value its own call and use the result.
advice.why: an assignment is not a program, so there is no argv0 for a rule to match; only a one-shot `VAR=value cmd` prefix is understood, and nothing on the allow list accepts one

advice.instead: nothing — installing changes the machine, so it prompts. Say which tool, which version, and why the task cannot proceed without it.
advice.why: an install is outside the repository and outlives the session

advice.instead: nothing — you are already in the project root. If you need another directory, most tools take a path argument (`git -C`, `rg PATH`, `--cwd`) and a path argument is one segment instead of two.
advice.why: `cd X && cmd` is two segments, and the second one is judged with no memory of the first, so the chain is only as allowed as its weakest half
